articles.title: ‘The flood is on its way’: How 400 Nepal students escaped in time
articles.summary: South Asia News: Morning assembly was about to begin at Bageshwori Higher Secondary School on August 26 when teachers learned that floodwaters were heading towards Bai.
articles.body: Morning assembly was about to begin at Bageshwori Higher Secondary School on August 26 when teachers learned that floodwaters were heading towards Baireni.Principal Prakash Malla told students to move to higher ground. Around 400 children were out of the school before the water arrived.Binita Ramtel had barely settled into her classroom and put down her bag when students were told to leave. "I had just arrived at the school, I had just kept my bag in the classroom and was preparing to come to the ground for the morning assembly, then the teachers made the announcement that the flood was on its way and asked us to evacuate, after which we fled from here," Binita told ANI while visiting her classroom.It was after 9am local time when the water entered Baireni. Students would normally have been arriving then for an assembly lasting about 15-20 minutes. Bageshwori Higher Secondary School stands close to the river.Principal orders students to higher groundA guardian living upstream had alerted the school about the approaching flood. Science teacher Dipendra Wagle said one of the staff members received information from Nuwakot as students were getting ready for physical training (PT) or assembly."When the students were preparing to attend the PT or the assembly, one of our teachers got information about the flood from Nuwakot. After that, our teacher Prakash Malla (Principal) announced from the office to get out of the school and all students ran away from here and are safe," he told ANI.Another warning about the water moving downstream reached Rajkumar Rimal through his spouse. Rimal, whose child attended the school, was working in a field at the time. His spouse told him that flooding had already hit the Betrawati River in Nuwakot.Speaking with ANI he said: "I was working in the field that day, and my spouse called me, warning that the Betrawati in Nuwakot had already been swept away by the flood and it is running downstream. The status of the students in school was my primary concern, as the two schools here are of direct concern and threat of the flood. I hurriedly came to the school and saw everyone was panicking and teachers were shifting the students to the safer grounds from here; I also helped them to evacuate students to the higher grounds successfully." He later joined the evacuation at the school.Bags remain on desks after evacuationWhen Binita returned almost a week later, the playground was covered in sand and her classroom in sludge and debris.The sudden departure was evident in what students had left behind. Bags remained on desks. Binita and her friend Prasamsha Magrati came across other students' damp belongings, along with tiffin boxes containing uneaten food.Marks left on the walls indicated both the level reached by the floodwater and the damage inside the school.Baireni lies on the Prithvi Highway. Flooding inundated the town on Wednesday, leaving deposits of mud and sand that reached as much as two metres above the river's level.Mud and sludge remained across the school premises almost a week later, while debris continued to give off a foul smell.Binita also lost belongings she used at school. "If it is provided by the local cooperatives; if not, then I am alive, I will buy it again," she said.17,000 children need humanitarian aidAround 17,000 children required humanitarian assistance after the August 26 floods, according to UNICEF estimates. The reported toll had crossed 900, with hundreds of people still missing.UNICEF appealed for USD 17.2 million to keep the emergency response going and support the initial recovery effort as assessments of overall needs continued.Relief teams and search operations remained active in the heavily affected districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading. For Bageshwori Higher Secondary School, there was still no clear date for classes to resume.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'No double standards on terrorism': PM Modi's message at SCO summit in presence of Pak PM Shehbaz Sharif
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday said there can be no “double standards” in the fight against terrorism and called for dismantling i.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday said there can be no “double standards” in the fight against terrorism and called for dismantling its entire ecosystem, including financing, recruitment, radicalisation and safe havens.Addressing the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit in Bishkek, PM Modi described terrorism as a “grave challenge to all of humanity” and said the fight against it cannot be limited to a mindset of “action-reaction”.“We must dismantle the entire ecosystem of terrorism--its financing, recruitment, radicalization, and safe havens. We must speak in one voice that there can be no place for double standards on this serious issue,” he said.“Those countries that use terrorism as an instrument of their policy, and provide shelter and support to terrorists, must be sent a strong message that terrorism cannot be a ‘strategic asset’ for anyone,” the Prime Minister added.He also outlined "Security, Connectivity and Opportunity" as the three pillars of India’s vision for the SCO, with peace and security forming the first pillar.“Our shared aspiration for a peaceful and secure Eurasia is also linked to peace and stability in Afghanistan,” he said, adding that India would continue its development and humanitarian assistance to the Afghan people.On the West Asia crisis, Modi said conflicts in one region can have repercussions across the world, affecting “energy security, maritime trade, and supply chains of the entire world”.“The countries of the Global South have to bear the maximum brunt of this. Therefore, India's call has been that the solution to all tensions and wars is not possible on the battlefield, but only through Dialogue and Diplomacy,” he said.The Prime Minister also flagged drug trafficking as a serious threat to the younger generation and regional security, calling for stronger cooperation through SCO mechanisms dealing with security threats, organised crime, information security and narcotics. “We must make them effective mediums for practical coordination and timely action,” PM Modi said.He further stressed that SCO cooperation should translate into tangible benefits for people, with people-to-people ties placed at the centre of the grouping’s future agenda.“The true measure of our success should be how many new opportunities our efforts have created for young people, how many new markets have opened up for our entrepreneurs, how much our farmers have benefited from technology, and how much better the lives of our citizens have become,” he said.Kyrgyzstan President Sadyr Japarov is hosting the summit and serving as its chairman. articles.title: A YouTuber spent 4 years helping strangers find lost relatives; then a DNA test gave him a 22.7% match with a 66-year-old Texas woman who turned out to be his long-lost sister
articles.summary: US News: Blair Clark and his wife Leah have spent more than four years on their YouTube show, The Leah and Blair Slog, helping people reconnect with relatives .
articles.body: Blair Clark and his wife Leah have spent more than four years on their YouTube show, The Leah and Blair Slog, helping people reconnect with relatives they’ve never known, or lost touch with. The couple, who live in the Philippines, have helped adoptees find biological parents and Amerasian Filipinos find fathers once stationed at U.S. naval and air bases. But in a remarkable twist Blair has recently become the seeker of a missing part of his own family history. According to a report by Upworthy, Blair was given a DNA testing kit from MyHeritage, a family history and genetic testing company. He signed up for the platform and found a 22.7% DNA match with a 66-year-old woman in San Antonio, Texas, named Fiona. The match suggested Fiona could be an aunt or a half-sister. As Blair started to look into the connection, the evidence was pointing more and more to an incredible conclusion: Fiona was his long-lost sister. The find was especially poignant as Blair had known a family secret since the age of 20. His mother, Isabel, told him that she'd had a child when she was 19, and she'd placed the baby for adoption.A family divided by social stigmaIsabel’s story was a painful truth faced by many unmarried mothers in the United Kingdom after the Second World War, states the news report. Women who had children out of wedlock were often stigmatized and in many cases pressured to give their children up for adoption. It also reports that around 200,000 mothers were forced to give children up for adoption in the 30 years after the war, during the UK's war-time generation. Isabel died aged 59 in 1999, never finding out that her daughter would be identified decades later. And then, Fiona was adopted shortly after birth and brought up in Scotland and Bermuda. Over the years she has worked in the oil industry, human resources and retail management. Ultimately, her life took her to Louisiana, Yemen and San Antonio, Texas. She later had two daughters, three grandsons and a great-grandson.66 years waiting for answersFiona opened a MyHeritage account about 10 years ago, leaving the door open for a family find. The long-awaited connection finally appeared after Blair joined the platform. The two then met over Zoom, where Fiona found out Blair was her brother, and she had three brothers in all. One of the most moving moments was when Fiona was shown a picture of Isabel. She'd never known her mother, but seeing her face suddenly gave a tangible connection to the woman whose identity had been a mystery all her life. Fiona’s similarity to their mother made the discovery all the more powerful for Blair. The picture helped cement his understanding that the woman he had known only in family lore for years had left behind another daughter.From helping others to finding his own familyThere was a strange irony in Blair’s discovery. For years he and Leah had sat behind the camera, helping strangers find family histories and witness emotional reunions. Suddenly, Blair was experiencing the same uncertainty, excitement and sense of closure as the people he had previously helped. The experience also gave him a greater appreciation of what those reunions meant to those involved, especially Fiona, who lived 65 years without knowing her biological identity or family. Now the newly discovered siblings are working to build the relationship they never had growing up. Blair lives in the Philippines and two of his brothers are in Australia. The four siblings hope to meet up in Thailand around the end of 2026, starting a new chapter for a family separated for more than six decades. A GoFundMe campaign is underway to help fund the reunion. Separated for a lifetime, the siblings now have a chance not only to learn of their common past but to build a future together, concludes the news report by Upworthy.Images Courtesy: Facebook and UpworthyCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1996, CNN founder Ted Turner bought a reported 558,000-acre New Mexico ranch; conservation work expanded its bison herd and restored about 30 miles of streams
articles.summary: US News: Discover how Ted Turner transformed Vermejo Park Ranch into a model of ecological restoration while reviving its bison population to over 1,200 and restoring essential habitats across 558,000 acres.
articles.body: In 1996, when CNN founder Ted Turner bought Vermejo Park Ranch from Pennzoil, he acquired an enormous private landscape in northern New Mexico and southern Colorado that had a long history of ranching, mining and intensive land uses. Reported to cover roughly 558,000 acres by High Country News, the property contains diverse habitat, ranging from semi-arid grasslands to alpine forests, that support vital populations of bison, elk, black bears and mountain lions. Over the decades that followed, Turner’s managers worked to restore parts of the overused landscape, with the ranch’s bison population eventually exceeding 1,200 animals and riparian areas along around 30 miles of streams undergoing restoration.Ted Turner’s conservation interests predated the Vermejo purchase, as he had already begun acquiring large Western ranches and building bison herds, but the newly acquired landscape gave him an unusually large area on which wildlife conservation, ranching and habitat restoration could occur simultaneously. The ranch was not converted into a conventional nature preserve; instead, the management approach opted to maintain productive uses while changing land-management practices to improve habitat and protect native species. This was reportedly a part of Turner’s broader effort to combine conservation with economic activity on his private ranches.A working ranch begins a long restoration effortHigh Country News described the property as overgrazed and overused and noted that the managers worked over many years to restore its ecological conditions. Furthermore, the size of the property allowed restoration work to take place across grasslands, forests, streams and wetlands while the ranch continued to operate as a working landscape.A NASA DEVELOP technical report, produced with Vermejo Ranch and Colorado Parks and Wildlife, noted that the ranch partnered with the US Fish and Wildlife Service and Colorado Parks and Wildlife on a large native-trout restoration project. Beginning in 2002, the work included wetland and riparian restoration and reintroduction of Rio Grande cutthroat trout in the Costilla Creek watershed. Additionally, the project used satellite and other remote sensing data to identify wetland and riparian regions where additional habitat restoration could be undertaken.The ranch’s conservation agreements also brought state and federal agencies into long-term habitat work in 2013. Notably, because Costilla Creek acts as an interstate waterway, the native trout restoration initiatives spanned a shared watershed matrix. The New Mexico Department of Game and Fish reported that the park ranch, the department, Colorado Parks and Wildlife and the US Fish and Wildlife Service jointly signed an agreement to safeguard the Rio Grande cutthroat trout. The initiative included removing non-native trout in parts of the watershed while allowing the ranch to continue agricultural and recreational uses.More than 1,200 bison have been restored in the landscapeBison became one of the most visible symbols of Turner’s conservation efforts. The CNN founder considered the species both an important part of the Great Plains ecosystem and a practical component of large-scale ranch management. At Vermejo, the restoration programme eventually brought the bison population to more than 1,200 animals.Independent academic research shed additional light on the size of the herd. A 2024 University of Nebraska-Lincoln master’s thesis examined the spatial ecology of American bison on Vermejo Park Ranch and documented a population of around 1,200 bison during 2022-23. The research analysed how bison movements and grazing patterns related to forage and landscape conditions on the ranch. Additionally, early conservation reports documented the restoration of riparian areas along about 30 miles of streams, while NASA and government records verify long-term wetland stability and provide satellite imaging confirmation of these remote mountain ecosystems.Conservation expanded beyond the ranch’s bison restorationIn 1997, Turner established the Turner Endangered Species Fund, which subsequently supported conservation projects that involved species like Mexican wolves and black-footed ferrets. Some of those projects occurred on Vermejo, while others were undertaken on Turner’s other ranches.Additionally, the ranch remained economically active, as activities like hunting, fishing, tourism and ranching continued alongside conservation work. According to the US Fish and Wildlife Service, the property contains 19 fishable lakes and more than 550,000 acres of habitat, while the ranch’s current materials describe about 30 miles of streams and a range of wildlife-based recreational opportunities.The restoration work continued beyond the earliest years of Turner’s ownership. In 2021, the CNN founder established the Turner Institute of Ecoagriculture, thus extending his interest in combining ecological restoration with productive land management.By the time of recent reporting, the property had become a long-running example of private conservation on a working landscape. Its transformation was not a single before-and-after event; instead, it involved changes to land use, restoration of riparian and wetland habitats, native fish recovery, reclamation of areas affected by historic mining and long-term management of a large bison herd.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Australian high school students collected more than 2,000 plastic bottles to form a greenhouse, 11 years later, the structure supplies food for the school's garden
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A project that began as an ecological lesson has transformed the lives of students at an Australian high school. In the country's capital of Canberra,.
articles.body: A project that began as an ecological lesson has transformed the lives of students at an Australian high school. In the country's capital of Canberra, students at the Richardson Primary School in south Canberra collected more than 2,000 plastic bottles and transformed them into the walls of a greenhouse that has been working efficiently for the past decade, as reported by ABC News. The project called Plastic Palace, was inaugurated on June 24, 2015, with a grant of AU$2,000 from the Teachers Mutual Bank Environment Fund. Eleven years later, the structure is still standing and provides food for the school's garden.The idea originated in 2012 with Kate Davis, a sixth-grade teacher at the school, who proposed to her students that they transform everyday waste into an educational resource. The bottle collection lasted for a year and a half, with participation from students, teachers and families from across the school. "At first, we thought 2,000 bottles would be enough, but the original plan grew in scale," explained Davis, who led the project from her classroom.In order to build the walls of the greenhouse, the bottles were cleaned and strung on columns attached to a wooden frame, mounted on the original earthen floor of the patio. Their translucent bodies allow light to pass through and protect the plants inside from the wind while the bottoms of the bottles are reused as pots for seedlings that are later transplanted to the garden. The construction combines hands-on learning with materials that would otherwise have ended up in a landfill.The grant given by the fund covered the cost of timber, tools and seeds and helped complete the construction. The greenhouse was officially opened on June 24, 2015, with the then Minister of Education for the Australian Capital Territory, Joy Burch, in attendance. "It's a fantastic example of reduce, reuse, and recycle," Burch said at the opening.The school's headteacher, Jason Borton, recalled how the students worked with their teacher until the greenhouse dream became a reality. What began as a one-class project ended up involving the entire school, and today the Plastic Palace remains an integral part of science classes, the school garden, and the chickens. The seedlings that sprout among the bottles are eventually transplanted into the outdoor garden beds."It has also helped them realise that something you use every day can be transformed into something else," summarised Kate Davis, the teacher who spearheaded the project from the year it was first proposed.Moreover, when it comes to nurturing the greenhouse plants, the vegetable patch and tending to the school's chooks, the students are in charge. "Really, they do everything in the garden. The classes come out to plant and they cultivate the food," said Borton. "The greenhouse is the breeding ground for the seedlings, then the students transfer them to the garden so they can see how food gets to the table."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: For more than four decades, George Divoky has worked from Cooper Island’s lone cabin; by 1989, the black guillemot colony he tracked had reached 200 breeding pairs
articles.summary: Rest of World News: George Divoky has spent nearly 11 cumulative years on Cooper Island, which is a remote sandbar off northern Alaska, and studied a colony of Mandt’s bl.
articles.body: George Divoky has spent nearly 11 cumulative years on Cooper Island, which is a remote sandbar off northern Alaska, and studied a colony of Mandt’s black guillemots. He first encountered the birds there in 1972, when a Coast Guard icebreaker dropped him off for a seabird survey and he found 10 breeding pairs nesting beneath debris left behind by the U.S. Navy. By 1989, the colony had grown to 200 breeding pairs.The island is about 35 kilometres southeast of Point Barrow, now known as Utqiaġvik, and has little infrastructure. Divoky worked alone for a large part of his study, and lived in a tent during the summer and used the island's only cabin as his base. His annual visits turned a small seabird survey into one of the longest-running records of an Arctic bird colony.The colony began under discarded Navy debrisDivoky arrived in 1972, and noticed that the black guillemots were nesting in cavities beneath ammunition boxes, floorboards and wooden planks abandoned by the Navy after the Korean War. The accessible nesting sites gave him an unusual opportunity to inspect nearly every nest on the island. He began creating additional nesting cavities from the discarded material, and the number of nest sites increased, and the colony expanded. A technical record prepared by the US Environmental Protection Agency says the colony grew from 10 breeding pairs in 1972 to as many as 220 pairs in 1988, with 200 breeding pairs recorded in 1989.Divoky counted active nests, recorded breeding success and followed individual birds through banding when he began returning in 1975. Because the guillemots nested in human-made cavities, researchers could inspect the available sites and determine how many contained eggs. The arrangement also made it possible to collect unusually detailed information about individual birds, since adults and chicks were banded, while measurements of growth, feeding and reproduction were recorded during the breeding season.A solitary summer routine became long-term researchAudubon's account of his research describes 43 consecutive years of summer visits by 2017, usually with Divoky living alone in a tent.He visited each nest, checked the chicks, weighed them and recorded their measurements, and also tracked which adults returned and which birds paired with one another.The resulting dataset covered the colony through periods when its numbers rose and then declined. Friends of Cooper Island describes the research as a largely solitary effort that has continued for almost five decades, with Divoky using occasional grants and personal resources to maintain the work.The long record became useful for a reason Divoky could not have established at the beginning of the project: it captured the colony before and during a period of rapid Arctic warming.Sea ice moved farther from the birdsMandt’s black guillemots are closely associated with Arctic sea ice. The birds could feed their chicks Arctic cod, a fatty fish that gathers around the ice edge, when ice remained near Cooper Island during the breeding season. As the surrounding waters warmed and summer sea ice retreated, Arctic cod became less available near the island. The guillemots increasingly turned to fourhorn sculpin, a fish of similar size but with a bonier body that is harder for chicks to digest. Audubon reported that chicks fed sculpin grew more slowly and were more likely to starve before fledging.The EPA's documentation of the Cooper Island dataset similarly identifies changes in sea ice and associated prey as important factors in the colony's decline. It notes that the colony's breeding-pair numbers can be used as an indicator of changes in the physical environment and marine ecosystem.From 200 pairs to a shrinking colonyAudubon reported that 85 pairs bred on Cooper Island in 2017 and produced 45 fledglings from 120 hatchlings, a level of reproduction that was insufficient to maintain the population. Polar bears that once remained on sea ice began appearing more frequently on Cooper Island as the ice retreated, while horned puffins also preyed on guillemot chicks. In 2009, Audubon reported, the two predators together accounted for 80% of chick deaths recorded that year.Divoky installed predator-resistant plastic nest cases in 2011, and the new cases replaced the original wooden nest structures and gave the birds more protection from predators while preserving the researchers' access to the nests. A later Pacific Seabird Group research summary reported 100 breeding pairs in 2016, compared with the colony's 200-pair level in 1989. It also described the long-running study as an annual record dating to 1975.The cabin remains a base for the studyFriends of Cooper Island still publishes field updates and research from the project, including records from recent breeding seasons. The Cooper Island record now spans more than five decades, from a colony of 10 pairs discovered beneath abandoned military debris to a population that reached about 200 breeding pairs before declining as Arctic conditions changed. The same small island remains the place where Divoky's annual measurements have documented that shift.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: What happens when a historic celebrity home is demolished? Richard Gere’s $10.75 million Connecticut estate is gone, but where did the 1938 oak library, marble fireplace, antique doorway and other pieces go?
articles.summary: Real Estate News: Richard Gere’s former New Canaan, Connecticut, home sat empty for less than a year before being demolished last year. In October 2024, Richard Gere, 7.
articles.body: Richard Gere’s former New Canaan, Connecticut, home sat empty for less than a year before being demolished last year. In October 2024, Richard Gere, 75, and his wife, Alejandra Gere, 42, sold their New Canaan, Conn., property for $10.75 million before relocating to Spain. By August 2025, the 1938 historic brick Georgian Colonial-style country manor was gone. The manor was reduced to an empty parcel of land, and the new owners plan to divide the plot into nine lots that could fit as many luxury homes.And just like that, the 87-year-old historic home was gone. The wrecking ball swept through what was once a six-bedroom house complete with a koi pond, a courtyard and enough architectural detail to make preservationists wince! So, before the trucks arrived, the salvage team sprang into action to rescue what could be saved. "We recently checked in, and the house has been taken down. We are grateful that the buyers allowed us time to salvage and get everything out,” salvage company owner Reggie Young told People.It’s been a year since the house was demolished. But what happened to the cerused oak library, Italian marble mantels and hand-carved stone doorways?The former celebrity ownersThe historic manor has seen many elite owners ever since it was built in 1938. Richard Gere and his wife purchased the Connecticut estate from legendary singer Paul Simon in 2022 for $10.8 million, a discount from its listing price. Simon and his wife, Edie Brickell, bought the property in 2002 for a whopping $16.5 million. The couple had owned it longer, watching their daughter Lulu grow up in its rooms. When Gere sold it two years later, he triggered a chain reaction that would ultimately undo nearly a century of history. No wonder Lulu reacted the way she did. In a since-deleted Instagram post, Lulu conveyed that she was not happy with the demolition. “Just in case anyone was wondering if I still hate Richard Gere—I do!" And she has her reasons for that.Gere sold it to the developer, SBP Homes, and they transformed the 32-acre lot into a nine-property luxury subdivision, turning it into the largest new residential project New Canaan has seen since 2007. The plot was turned into a nine-lot subdivision ranging in size from 2.2 to 4.8 acres, according to CT Insider. The plan was to sell the land in parcels, empty. They knew wealthy buyers would buy it and build their own vision. "We’re very excited about this project. From the beginning, our goal was to thoughtfully accommodate a wide range of interests in how the property would be developed," SBP Homes project manager Adam Sherer said in a statement.And just like any other developer project, there is rarely room for sentiment or preservation. So, no, the developer had no sentiment for Lulu’s childhood home, even though it was historic. The cost of maintaining a 1938 Colonial while carving a subdivision around it didn't pencil out. The legal complications of heritage designation were even more complicated. So demolition was the only way forward for the developers.What got savedIn May 2025, a New York salvage company called Hudson Valley House Parts was called in to salvage parts of the 1938 six-bedroom brick Colonial, according to Realtor.com. "It's so important that the developers allowed the project to be salvaged," Young told People. He added that it was ‘a real shame’ that the house was being torn down. "Once the stuff is gone, it's never coming back,” he told Realtor.com.The firm managed to rescue various unique elements from the property, including an oak library, nautical-themed bay windows, limestone and marble mantels and other architectural features. They were too good to be torn out in the demolition.All these were priceless in the market, as high-end homebuyers often seek to add historical character to new spaces. So there is a demand for marble mantels, refurbished wood flooring and antique hardware. However, there's a gap between demand and actual execution. Most of these demolished homes never get properly salvaged; as a result, only 20 to 30 per cent of construction and demolition debris is recovered for reuse, according to the Environmental Protection Agency.However, Gere’s house had better luck. The octagonal bluestone patio, complete with what Hudson Valley House Parts described as ‘exceptional patina’, was lifted and palletised. The colonial window sashes went into storage. A limestone mantel travelled to a buyer in New Orleans. The ornate doorway with fanned glass and Egyptian columns found a new home in a Colonial Revival renovation in Indiana."Mantels are popular," Young said. He added that "a good marble mantel usually goes for $4,000 to $8,000."Other parts of the home that were salvaged include the nautical motifs made of steel, the mid-century bay windows, a limestone mantel and a marble mantel; a complete cerused oak library with a curved fireplace and built-in wall panelling; exterior stone steps with an iron railing; a portico; and the entire entryway with its arched jamb, door surround and panelled walls. The bluestone edge of the koi pond was also rescued.The oak library panels, the stone patio and the marble mantel may find another house. But the 1938 house itself, the one with 87 years of history, is erased, and the land now awaits a new one.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: In 2016, Frank and Monica Woll bought two tiny Florida Keys islands for semi-retirement; hurricanes soon washed away much of them
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Frank and Monica Woll purchased the Molasses Keys in 2016 for a peaceful retirement, but hurricanes threatened their effort to preserve the islands. Discover their ongoing fight against erosion and commitment to conservation in the Florida Keys.
articles.body: Frank and Monica Woll bought two small islands south of the Seven Mile Bridge in the Florida Keys, known locally as the Molasses Keys, taking on the property in the mid 2010s according to accounts from visitors and local boaters. After decades running a paddling and outfitting business on Key Largo, the couple wanted a quieter retirement caring for a patch of mangrove and sand instead of running a shop. Instead, they saw how quickly a low-lying Florida Keys island can lose ground after a major hurricane, a lesson that has played out repeatedly in the decade since, from Hurricane Irma in 2017 through to the present day.A modest preserve, not a resortThe islands the Wolls bought were never likely to be developed conventionally. The islands' own preserve materials describe a handful of low-lying islands considered environmentally sensitive, home to nesting birds, several species of crab and stands of state-protected black, red and white mangrove. Rather than build anything permanent, the couple treated the purchase as a stewardship project, setting up a system that let day visitors and the occasional camper register in advance, on the condition that they left the islands exactly as they found them. Frank Woll's ownership of the preserve was confirmed in local reporting describing him ferrying emergency responders from the islands to the scene of a boat crash near the bridge in 2025. That low-key approach suited the couple, who had spent years serving paddlers and boaters through their outfitting business before choosing to spend retirement on conservation.Storms that reshape land within hoursOwning land in the lower Keys, however modest, comes with an exposure to hurricanes that few other retirement projects carry. The islands sit on the Atlantic side of the archipelago, in the path of major storms that have long crossed the region, and each hurricane season brings the risk of losing ground that took centuries to build. Scientists who study similar low-lying Florida Bay islands have documented how dramatic that loss can be in a single event. A study from the US Geological Survey comparing elevation measurements on nearby islands before and after Hurricane Irma in 2017 found that the island closest to the storm's path lost between 32 and 42 per cent of the width of its eastern berm, along with a meaningful share of its vegetated cover.Although no equivalent survey has measured exactly how much shoreline the Molasses Keys have been lost since 2016, but the islands sit in the same exposed conditions described by the study: low to the water, thinly vegetated in places, and dependent on mangrove roots to hold sediment against wind and surge. When a hurricane tracks close enough, the same forces that shaped the islands over centuries can strip away ground in a single tide cycle, leaving landowners to assess the damage after the water recedes.Rebuilding by hand, one storm at a timeThe islands have not disappeared, but they have shrunk and reshaped considerably since the Wolls took them on, and for the couple, erosion control became an ongoing part of caring for the islands rather than a one-time repair. Their approach has reportedly involved simple, manual methods, stacking rock to slow further erosion along the most exposed shorelines and replanting mangrove seedlings in the hope that new root systems will eventually do the work that machinery cannot. Mangrove restoration of this kind is notoriously difficult on small, storm-battered islands, since young saplings often struggle with salinity shock and tidal exposure long before their roots are established enough to hold sediment in place.Even so, the Wolls have treated each setback as a reason to keep working rather than give up on the project. Their islands show what it means to hold onto a piece of coastline in a part of Florida where hurricanes can bring sudden, severe flooding and erosion. Whether that stewardship can keep up with erosion in the decades ahead remains to be seen.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Indonesia wildfire crisis: 19 companies under scrutiny as 2 lakh hectares burnt
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Indonesia's wildfire crisis has burned 202,010 hectares of forest and land between January and July, while authorities are inspecting 19 companies lin.
articles.body: Indonesia's wildfire crisis has burned 202,010 hectares of forest and land between January and July, while authorities are inspecting 19 companies linked to fires covering 11,047 hectares within their concessions across seven provinces.Nearly 95,000 hectares burned in July alone, against 107,465 hectares recorded during the first six months of the year, according to Forestry Ministry data.Indonesia's Health Ministry said 10.67 million people across seven provinces had been affected by the fires as of August 27. It recorded 13,449 cases of acute respiratory infection, including 4,082 cases on August 27.19 firms face inspectionsOfficials identified 42 concession holders considered at high risk of fires. Fires covering 11,047 hectares were found within concessions managed by 19 of them, while authorities were continuing to examine the other 23.Environment Ministry official Rizal Irawan said strict-liability rules apply to fires within concession areas regardless of whether they were accidental or deliberate, news agency Reuters reported.Police have also arrested 72 people in connection with recent forest and peatland fires. Most are suspected of deliberately burning land as a cheaper clearing method, while investigators are separately examining whether any companies directed or financed such activity, news agency AP reported.Fires recur during Indonesia's dry season, with deliberate burning to clear land for agriculture and plantations among the causes. Peat fires can persist below ground, making them particularly difficult to extinguish.11,567 personnel deployed in South SumatraIn South Sumatra alone, 11,567 personnel, including military, police, disaster-response teams, firefighters and volunteers, had been deployed as of August 31, according to BNPB.The government has also deployed 34 aircraft for water-bombing operations, while more than 1,400 volunteers have been sent to fire-affected areas, news agency Reuters reported.BNPB recorded six new forest and land fires between August 30 and 31, with incidents reported in East Kalimantan, Central Java, South Sulawesi and North Maluku.In South Sumatra, 67.06 hectares remained under firefighting or close monitoring as of August 30. BNPB said 18.36 hectares had been extinguished, while another 48.7 hectares remained in the cooling-down phase.Authorities are also carrying out cloud-seeding and other weather-modification operations in an effort to induce rain over fire-prone areas. Ground and aerial operations have been stepped up as haze has reduced air quality across several provinces and spread into neighbouring Malaysia.Seven orangutans rescued in fire zonesThe fires have also affected wildlife in Kalimantan, the Indonesian part of Borneo. An adult male orangutan was found in a weakened condition near a fire zone in Ketapang, West Kalimantan, and treated after exposure to heavy smoke.The orangutan, named Sampurna, suffered hypoxia that a wildlife foundation linked to smoke exposure. Veterinarians also suspected an acute respiratory infection. Sampurna was among seven orangutans rescued during this year's fires, news agency Reuters reported.BMKG said satellite monitoring on August 31 found the largest concentration of high-confidence hotspots in Kalimantan, followed by Sumatra, Papua and Maluku.The meteorological agency expects hot and relatively dry weather to persist in early September, although local rain remains possible, and said smoke could spread into surrounding areas depending on wind direction.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: CJP calls off Sept 5 march after SC quashes all FIRs against protesters on Centre's request
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janata Party on Tuesday withdrew its call for a march on September 5 after Supreme Court, on the Centre's request, quashed all FI.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janata Party on Tuesday withdrew its call for a march on September 5 after Supreme Court, on the Centre's request, quashed all FIRs registered across the country against students who participated in the NEET protests."I want to state that in view of the positive assurances of the government of India and the judicial sanctity bestowed upon them today, and in view of the order being passed by this court, the CJP deems it appropriate to withdraw the call for the march on September 5 and looks forward to compliance with today's order," CJP co-convener Sourav Das said during a hearing in the Supreme Court.This comes after Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre and Delhi Police, informed the apex court that the Centre remains committed to fulfilling all three assurances given to the leadership of CJP during the meeting between the Centre and the party.What were the three assurancesThe first assurance was that the Centre would not pursue FIRs registered between July 20 and July 25.The second assurance was that no fresh FIRs would be registered in connection with the matter.The third assurance was that the government would pay compensation to students who died by suicide allegedly in connection with the NEET paper leak."Centre is committed to honour the assurance given to the CJP leaders to provide compensation to the families of students who died by suicide after NEET exam cancellation; however, 3 months needed to work out the modalities," Mehta told SC."As of now, we are committed to fulfilling all three assurances," he added.Earlier on Monday, Centre moved the apex court seeking to quash FIR's registered against the student protesters with alleged violence during protests over the NEET paper leak in Delhi and other states.Solicitor general Tushar Mehta mentioned the plea before a bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant on Monday, seeking the court’s intervention in the matter.The Centre has urged the Supreme Court to exercise its extraordinary powers under Article 142 of the Constitution to quash the FIRs registered against the protesting students.Also read: 'Keeping future of students in mind': Nadda after quashing of FIRs against NEET protesters.Why CJP had called for Sept 5 marchCJP had called for a protest march in Delhi on September 5, Teachers' Day. It had accused the Centre of failing to honour the promises made on July 25 to persuade the group to withdraw its 36-day agitation against irregularities in exams and the NEET paper leak.According to the CJP, the march was to be led by families of students who committed suicide following the cancellation of the NEET exam and the subsequent re-test, as well as those who were allegedly subjected to police excesses during the July agitation.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1965, Bob Hope bought a 212-acre former Hollywood movie ranch; after thousands of Westerns were filmed there, plans emerged to turn much of it into a park
articles.summary: US News: In 1965, comedian and actor Bob Hope bought Corriganville, a 212-acre former Hollywood movie ranch in Simi Valley, California. The property had spent .
articles.body: In 1965, comedian and actor Bob Hope bought Corriganville, a 212-acre former Hollywood movie ranch in Simi Valley, California. The property had spent decades serving the film industry, providing locations for thousands of films, television programmes and commercials. It also operated as a tourist attraction, where visitors could explore Western-style sets and watch stunt performances. Hope renamed the property Hopetown, and plans later emerged to develop much of the land. However, the former movie ranch took a different path. Fires destroyed many of its remaining structures during the 1970s, but much of the property remained undeveloped. In 1988, the City of Simi Valley purchased 190 acres and converted the land into Corriganville Park, preserving part of a site that had played a major role in Hollywood's Western filmmaking history.Why did Bob Hope buy the 212-acre Hollywood movie ranchBob Hope purchased Corriganville in 1965 and renamed it ‘Hopetown.’ The sale marked the end of the site's period as a public movie ranch and tourist attraction. The property's future soon shifted towards development. Atlas Obscura reports that the sale was connected to plans for housing on the 212-acre site. Those plans reflected a broader change in the property's role. Rather than continuing as a dedicated film and entertainment venue, the land was increasingly viewed as an area with development potential. However, much of the site was not immediately transformed. This would later become significant when efforts were made to preserve a large section of the former ranch.Corriganville journey of becoming a Hollywood movie ranchActor and stuntman Ray ‘Crash’ Corrigan bought the land in 1937. According to Classic Movie Hub, Corrigan was already established in Western films and had appeared in the ‘Three Mesquiteers’ series. The site began operating as a movie ranch in 1938. Its open landscape and rock formations made it suitable for productions requiring outdoor locations. According to Flying Dawn Marie, Corriganville was used for an estimated 3,000 to 3,500 films, television programmes and commercials. Several leading Western stars worked there, including John Wayne, Gene Autry and Roy Rogers. However, the ranch was not restricted to Western productions. Films associated with the site included ‘The Creature from the Black Lagoon,’ ‘The African Queen’ and ‘The Three Musketeers.’ Television productions such as ‘The Lone Ranger,’ ‘The Adventures of Rin Tin Tin’ and ‘Star Trek’ also used the location.Corriganville turning into a tourists attractionCorriganville eventually expanded beyond its role as a filming location. According to Classic Movie Hub, it operated as a Western-themed tourist attraction between 1949 and 1965. Visitors could explore the sets and watch stunt performances. They could also see the fort constructed for John Ford's 1948 film ‘Fort Apache.’ Flying Dawn Marie reports that the attraction included stagecoach rides and staged shoot-outs. The site featured a Western street called Silvertown, with buildings designed to resemble a typical frontier settlement. These included shops, stables, a church and a schoolhouse. Corriganville also had facilities designed specifically for filmmaking. A man-made lake was used for water scenes, while a specially constructed room with thick windows enabled underwater filming. Classic Movie Hub reports that the lake was used for productions including the ‘Jungle Jim’ series.Destruction caused by fire at the ranchMuch of what remained at the former ranch was destroyed by brush fires during the 1970s. Classic Movie Hub reports that several structures were lost due to major fires in 1971 and 1979. The destruction removed many of the buildings that had once formed Corriganville's elaborate film and tourist sets. However, some physical remains survived. Concrete foundations, stonework and other structures were left behind. The man-made lake and the site's underwater filming facility also remained. These remnants would later become part of the landscape preserved within the park. Although most of the original sets disappeared, evidence of the site's earlier use was not completely lost.How did the former movie ranch become a public parkIn 1988, the City of Simi Valley purchased 190 acres of the former ranch. According to Flying Dawn Marie, the land was subsequently converted into Corriganville Park. The purchase protected a substantial portion of the old property from further development and opened it to the public. Classic Movie Hub notes that the park now includes hiking trails and picnic areas. The surviving foundations and other remnants provide a link to the property's previous role in the film industry.The park is now primarily an outdoor recreation area, but its history remains visible in parts of the landscape. Corriganville's history changed direction several times over five decades. It began as a working movie ranch, developed into a tourist attraction and later faced plans for housing development. Fires then destroyed much of what remained of its famous sets. The 1988 purchase by the City of Simi Valley gave most of the surviving land a new future. Today, Corriganville Park serves as a public space while retaining traces of the movie ranch that once hosted thousands of productions and some of Hollywood's best-known performers.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Idaho is building a $20.8 million wildlife highway crossing to help deer migrate under a busy highway without losing lives
articles.summary: US News: The construction of a new wildlife underpass in southeast Idaho is about to be completed, after the public, nonprofit agencies, conservation groups an.
articles.body: The construction of a new wildlife underpass in southeast Idaho is about to be completed, after the public, nonprofit agencies, conservation groups and government agencies pushed for years to protect migrating wildlife herds and drivers, according to a report by Idaho Capital Sun.To save animal and human livesThe Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass is expected to be completed this fall along US Highway 30, south of Montpelier in Bear Lake County, public officials and conservationists announced jointly this week. The wildlife crossing features three underpasses and extensive fencing on either side of the project to guide animals such as deer to the crossing. “We were seeing just all kinds of problems there; we were losing at least 100 deer a year,” Idaho Transportation Department public information officer Justin Smith said in an interview Wednesday. “Over 10 years, that is 1,000 animals we know we lost.”Officials also said those collisions cost drivers and taxpayers millions of dollars every year. “Our primary concern is the safety of the travelling public. Whether they are going through a construction zone or whether they are in a wildlife area, we want to keep people safe on our highways, and this is part of that effort,” Smith said.The underpass represents a partnership between the Idaho Transportation Department, Idaho Department of Fish and Game, the Greater Yellowstone Coalition, the Idaho Conservation League, and Bear Lake County, officials said. “Rocky Point shows what’s possible when agencies, conservation, sporting groups, and local communities work toward the same goal,” Matt Lucia, Idaho conservation manager at the Greater Yellowstone Coalition, said in a written statement. “[The Greater Yellowstone Coalition] has been part of this project for years — contributing time, energy, and funds toward the effort. The next step is making sure the federal funding that made this project possible stays available.”To build the crossing, the Idaho Transportation Department secured a $20.8 million grant from the Federal Highway Administration's Wildlife Crossing Pilot Program. Funding comes from the federal Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act that was passed by Congress and signed into law by former President Joe Biden in 2021. The federal grant was estimated to cover 98% of the construction costs, but the project may come in under budget, allowing the state to return some of the money to the Federal Highway Administration, Smith said.More wildlife crossings in Idaho?Interestingly, the Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass near Montpelier is the second major wildlife highway crossing in Idaho. In 2023, crews built the Cervidae Peak Wildlife Overpass on Idaho Highway 21 near Lucky Peak, between Boise and Idaho City. The Cervidae overpass features more than one mile of big game fencing to direct the animals to the safe crossing.Fish and Game officials installed a wildlife camera at the crossing to document how it is working. In 2024, state officials posted a time-lapse video showing more than 1,000 deer safely using the Cervidae Peak Wildlife Overpass between Oct. 17, 2024, and Dec. 18, 2024.Smith added that officials with the Idaho Transportation Department are studying other highway corridors with heavy wildlife populations, and the state is open to pursuing additional wildlife crossings. “It is something that as Idaho’s population continues to grow, we need to look at ways to protect drivers and protect the wildlife,” Smith said. “It’s something we continue to look at.”“We’re always open to doing what needs to be done for the safety of the travelling public; that is our primary concern,” Smith added. “We will continue to look at these projects as ways to improve the safety on our highways.” The Idaho Legislature has also called for more wildlife crossings. In March, the Idaho Legislature adopted Senate Concurrent Resolution 124.The resolution encourages the Idaho Legislature, Idaho’s congressional delegation, the governor, the Idaho Transportation Department, and Fish and Game to recognise and support wildlife corridors to improve public safety and protect big game migration corridors.“The Legislature strongly supports the advancement of public safety and conservation of Idaho’s big game migration corridors through the development and implementation of wildlife crossings where appropriate and supported by local communities,” the resolution states.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Janmashtami 2026: When will the festival be celebrated? September 4 or 5; Pooja muhurat, timings, when to break the fast, rituals, everything you need to know
articles.summary: Trending News: Janmashtami marks the birth of Lord Krishna, the 8th incarnation of Lord Vishnu, which is celebrated with immense fervour and festive spirit.Every yea.
articles.body: Janmashtami marks the birth of Lord Krishna, the 8th incarnation of Lord Vishnu, which is celebrated with immense fervour and festive spirit.Every year around this time, the same question comes up in group chats and family circles, compelling us to ask: Is Janmashtami today or tomorrow?Sometimes, calendars, apps, and even temples list two different dates for the same festival; that is why this confusion comes up.Janmashtami falls on the eighth day of Krishna Paksha, the waning phase of the moon, in the Hindu month of Bhadrapada, which usually falls in August or September on the Gregorian calendar.Why is Janmashtami celebrated?Janmashtami celebrates the birth of Lord Krishna, believed to be the eighth avatar of Lord Vishnu, born to save the world from evil.The story goes back to King Kansa of Mathura, a cruel ruler and Lord Krishna’s maternal uncle, who learned of a prophecy that the eighth child of his sister Devaki would be the one to kill him. Terrified, Kansa imprisoned Devaki and her husband Vasudev, killing each of their children as they were born.But when the eighth child, Krishna, was born at midnight, something miraculous happened. The prison guards fell asleep, chains loosened, and Vasudev was able to carry the newborn Krishna across the flooded Yamuna River to safety in Gokul, where he was raised secretly by foster parents, Yashoda and Nanda.Krishna grew up to fulfill the prophecy, eventually defeating Kansa and restoring peace and righteousness, or dharma, to the kingdom.That's why Janmashtami is celebrated at midnight; it marks the exact moment Krishna was born and hope quietly triumphed over tyranny.When is Janmashtami 2026: September 4 or Sep 5, 2026?In 2026, that eighth day, the Ashtami Tithi, begins at 2:25 am on September 4 and runs until 12:13 am on September 5, according to Drik Panchang. Since Lord Krishna is believed to have been born at midnight, the festival's most important ritual naturally falls after the clock strikes twelve, which is exactly why September 5 keeps showing up alongside September 4 in most Janmashtami coverage.The festival will officially be celebrated on Friday, September 4, but because the most sacred rituals happen well past midnight, the celebrations will naturally go into September 5 as well.September 4 is observed as the main Janmashtami day, with the grand midnight celebration, Nishita Puja, carrying the festival into the early hours of September 5.Here are the Nishita Pooja Muhurats across various cities in India from Sept 4 into Sept 5:New Delhi: 11:57 PM – 12:43 AMMumbai: 12:14 AM – 1:01 AMPune: 12:10 AM – 12:57 AMChennai: 11:45 PM – 12:31 AMJaipur: 12:03 AM – 12:49 AMHyderabad: 11:52 PM – 12:38 AMGurgaon: 11:58 PM – 12:44 AMChandigarh: 11:59 PM – 12:45 AMKolkata: 11:13 PM – 11:59 PM (Sept 4)Bengaluru: 11:55 PM – 12:42 AMAhmedabad: 12:16 AM – 1:02 AMNoida: 11:57 PM – 12:42 AMWhen to Break the Fast (Parana)Most devotees who observe a strict Janmashtami vrat break their fast only after the midnight Nishita Puja is complete, once Krishna's symbolic birth has been marked. Some others prefer to wait until after sunrise the next morning.Janmashtami 2026: How is the festival celebrated, rituals to follow and moreThe day typically begins with devotees observing a Nirjala or Phalahar vrat, abstaining from grains and pulses, and eating fruits, milk, and water for those doing a lighter fast.Through the day, people visit temples, sing bhajans, meditate, and prepare for the midnight celebration, decorating temples by arranging jhankis. At night, devotees bathe and dress an idol of Bal Gopal (infant Krishna), decorate a cradle, and offer panchamrit along with makhan-mishri, butter mixed with rock sugar, as the primary offering, often placed along with a Tulsi leaf. Once the Nishita Puja concludes, devotees break their fast with these offerings.The main attraction of the festival is Dahi HandiThe festivities don't end at midnight either. The next day marks the Nandotsav celebrations in Krishna temples, along with the energetic Dahi Handi tradition, where teams form human pyramids to break pots of curd suspended overhead. This custom is especially popular in Maharashtra.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: In 2014, a Colorado couple bought land to build a family ranch; by 2025 bird species had risen from 29 to 37 and grassland-bird detections doubled from 178 to 356
articles.summary: US News: When Lance and Lisa Wheeler bought land in Colorado to build a family ranch, their ambition was to raise healthy food and create a sustainable way of .
articles.body: When Lance and Lisa Wheeler bought land in Colorado to build a family ranch, their ambition was to raise healthy food and create a sustainable way of farming. More than a decade later, their land is also becoming a refuge for grassland birds. According to Audubon Rockies, which published the couple’s story on August 31, 2026, bird species recorded at their Rafter W Ranch increased from 29 in 2019 to 37 in 2025, while grassland-bird detections doubled from 178 to 356. The numbers offer a striking glimpse of what can happen when livestock production and conservation are managed together.From a childhood cowboy dream to a real ranchWheeler grew up in a Los Angeles suburb but dreamed of becoming a cowboy. His family had raised cattle in Texas for generations, although his own idea of ranching initially came more from watching Bonanza than experiencing life on a working ranch. That changed when he and Lisa began raising grass-fed meat, poultry and eggs on a small property in Elizabeth, Colorado, in the early 1990s.As they learned more about regenerative agriculture, they began thinking bigger. In 2014, the couple purchased land in Elbert County. Two years later, they acquired the neighbouring property and home. Today, their family-run operation, Rafter W Ranch, produces grass-fed beef, poultry and eggs, which it sells through an online ordering platform.But the Wheelers increasingly came to see that healthy livestock depended on something bigger: healthy land. “We’re not just raising meat, we’re actually farming grass,” Lance said, according to Audubon Rockies.The ranch became bird-friendlyIn 2018, Rafter W Ranch became certified through Audubon Conservation Ranching, a programme that promotes habitat management, environmental sustainability and animal welfare on working ranches.The Wheelers use adaptive and rotational grazing, moving cattle strategically across the property. Rather than allowing animals to graze the entire landscape uniformly, the approach creates areas with different grass heights. That variation matters for wildlife because different bird species depend on different kinds of grassland habitat.The ranch is now home to Western Meadowlarks, American Kestrels, Upland Sandpipers, Lark Buntings, Vesper Sparrows and Loggerhead Shrikes, among other species. The family also raises free-range chickens. The birds follow cattle in a mobile coop, picking through manure and helping incorporate it into the soil.Bird numbers tell the storyThe Wheelers have been monitoring the ranch alongside their conservation work, and the results have been encouraging.Audubon’s surveys found that species richness, the number of different bird species recorded, rose from 29 in 2019 to 37 in 2025.Grassland-bird detections increased from 178 to 356 over the same period. The ranch’s Bird-Friendliness Index, an Audubon measure incorporating bird abundance, diversity and resilience, also increased by about 4% annually, representing a cumulative rise of 26% since monitoring began.Audubon Conservation Ranching Director Dusty Downey attributed the progress largely to the Wheelers’ adaptive grazing practices and willingness to adjust their methods based on research and observations.Farming for the futureThe Wheelers’ work extends beyond grazing. Their ranch has participated in soil-health monitoring, erosion-control projects and efforts designed to improve water infiltration and resilience during drought. They have also opened the property for educational programmes, including bird walks and youth ranch experiences.For Lance, the work has changed his childhood idea of what being a cowboy meant. “Ranching is the most rewarding and the most humbling work that I’ve ever done,” he said.What began as a family’s effort to build a ranch has gradually become something larger: a working landscape where cattle, crops, soil and wildlife are managed as parts of the same ecosystem. And the bird surveys offer a measurable sign that the approach is making a difference, eight additional bird species recorded in six years, and twice as many grassland-bird detections.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Watch: 'Driverless' car crashes into police van after internet outage in Islamabad
articles.summary: Pakistan News: A remotely operated driverless car crashed into a police van in Islamabad after losing its internet connection during a demonstration, with footage of.
articles.body: A remotely operated driverless car crashed into a police van in Islamabad after losing its internet connection during a demonstration, with footage of the incident going viral and sparking a wave of memes online.According to local media, the incident took place at D-Chowk, a high-security area in the Pakistani capital, where journalist Muhammad Aalijah was recording a video of a technology-based automated-driving system developed by Abbottabad-based technology enthusiast Ehsan Zafar. The car was being controlled remotely over the internet when a sudden connectivity failure caused its steering to malfunction.Footage shared by Aalijah shows him sitting in the front passenger seat as he explains the vehicle's features while it moves along the road. The remotely controlled steering wheel then appears to lose control, sending the car towards a police van parked nearby.Aalijah can be seen attempting to stop the vehicle by pulling the handbrake, but the car continues moving and bumps into the police vehicle.Aalijah later told Dawn that he had been asked by Zafar to report on his technology-based automated-driving innovation. He attributed the crash to a "technical fault" triggered by an internet disruption.“Everything was fine until a technical fault occurred due to an internet disruption, causing the car to go out of control and crash into a police vehicle,” he said.According to Aalijah, the vehicle was operated remotely through internet and satellite connections. The loss of the internet connection during the demonstration caused the car to become uncontrollable.In a social media post on Monday, Aalijah sought to clarify that his video was not intended to ridicule Zafar or undermine his work.“The sole purpose was to raise awareness and urge people to remain cautious until any new experiment or technology has been thoroughly tested, proven safe and established as a complete success,” he said.“This was a message of caution, not an attempt to discredit anyone.”Aalijah also warned that the technology was not yet ready to be considered completely reliable.“The vehicle was being operated through satellite and internet connections, but during external control, it went out of control as soon as the internet connection was disconnected and collided with a police vehicle,” he wrote.He said the relatively low traffic at D-Chowk limited the potential consequences of the malfunction, but warned that a similar failure on a busy road could have been far more serious.“If the same situation had occurred on a busy road, the consequences could have been extremely dangerous, even fatal,” he said.“This video is not criticism; it is a responsible effort to raise awareness and issue a warning by all means, experiment, but ensure safety first,” he added.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: Pakistan News: A court in Pakistan on Tuesday allowed a 21-year-old Hindu woman to return to her parents after she told the magistrate that she wished to go home of .
articles.body: A court in Pakistan on Tuesday allowed a 21-year-old Hindu woman to return to her parents after she told the magistrate that she wished to go home of her own free will, days after her family alleged that she had been abducted and pressured to convert to Islam and marry a Muslim man, news agency PTI reported.Shirimati Reeta, a resident of Rana Rajput Colony in Khipro tehsil of Sindh’s Sanghar district, went missing from her hometown last week, according to a complaint filed by her brother Ravi Shankar. He alleged that CCTV footage showed unidentified people taking Reeta from the family home along with valuables and mobile phones on August 24.According to the complaint, Reeta was taken to Gujranwala in Punjab, some 80 kms from Lahore, where she was allegedly pressured to convert to Islam and marry Nazeer Hussain, who was already married.'Want to return home'Punjab Police later recovered Reeta and produced her before a judicial magistrate on Monday. The investigating officer sought to place her in Darul Aman, a state-run shelter, claiming that she was unwilling to return to her parents.Her lawyers, Asad Jamal and Kheta Ram, opposed the request and told the court that Reeta wanted to return home with her brother, who was present in court, a court official said.The magistrate then asked Reeta to record her statement under oath. “In her statement, Reeta said that she wanted to return to her parents’ home of her own free will,” the official said.The court subsequently allowed Reeta to leave with her brother and made him responsible for her safe custody and transportation back to the family home in Sanghar.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: Karachi's electricity crisis has intensified, with residents in several parts of the city reporting outages lasting up to 24 hours. Rights activists in Pakistan have warned that prolonged loadshedding is placing a growing burden on low-income families.According to Dawn, the issue was raised at a press conference at the Karachi Press Club organised by the Civil Society Collective for Clean Energy for Karachi. Speakers said extended power cuts were disrupting basic household activities, education and work, while also worsening access to water and affecting hygiene.Residents of North Karachi, Nazimabad and parts of Gulistan-i-Jauhar reported between 16 and 24 hours of loadshedding, ANI said. Protests and traffic disruptions were also reported in Lyari and other parts of the old city during the week beginning August 24.The speakers cited K-Electric's published outage schedule, saying more than 615 feeders were listed for power cuts of up to 12 hours a day. They claimed this could affect nearly a third of the city's feeders.Qazi Khizer of the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan said the prolonged outages were having a particularly severe impact on working-class communities.He said electricity shortages were also contributing to rising mental stress and argued that reliable electricity "should be treated as an essential service rather than a privilege".Karachi Union of Journalists president Tahir Hassan Khan questioned whether K-Electric's privatisation had delivered the improvements promised to consumers.He said claims of technological and operational progress had not translated into "dependable electricity supplies".Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Imran Khan, wife Bushra Bibi get slight relief as Pak HC bars solitary confinement
articles.summary: Pakistan News: A Pakistan high court on Tuesday directed authorities at Rawalpindi Jail to ensure that former prime minister Imran Khan and his wife Bushra Bibi are .
articles.body: A Pakistan high court on Tuesday directed authorities at Rawalpindi Jail to ensure that former prime minister Imran Khan and his wife Bushra Bibi are not held in solitary confinement. The ruling also set out provisions for Khan's family meetings, phone calls, reading material and medical care.The Islamabad High Court (IHC), while hearing petitions challenging the couple's alleged solitary confinement, directed the jail authorities to allow Khan's family members to meet him in line with prison rules and arrange telephone conversations with his sons.Justice Khadim Hussain Soomro also ordered the jail to provide Khan with newspapers and books every day and ensure access to medical facilities as prescribed under jail rules. Rawalpindi's Aiala jail superintendent has been asked to implement the directions and submit a compliance report within 15 days, according to the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).The court had earlier reserved its verdict on August 6 on separate petitions filed by Khan's sister Aleema Khanum and Bushra Bibi's daughter Mubashra Khawar Maneka. The IHC also held the petitions challenging the alleged solitary confinement to be maintainable.The 73-year-old cricketer-turned-politician and his wife have been in custody since August 2023 and is serving prison terms in corruption and related cases. Khan's Tehreek-e-Insaf party and supporters have maintained that the cases are politically motivated, while the government has rejected allegations of mistreatment.Bushra Bibi was first jailed in January 2024 after being convicted in a corruption-related case. She was released on bail in October that year after nearly nine months in custody but was arrested again in January 2025 following another corruption conviction. She remains at Adiala Jail.The IHC order comes as Khan's detention and medical treatment remain the subject of separate proceedings before the Supreme Court.On Monday, the Supreme Court declined an application by Khan's sister Uzma Khan seeking an early hearing of her contempt petition against government officials over the alleged failure to comply with an earlier order concerning his transfer to a private hospital, Dawn reported.Pakistan's Supreme Court had on August 18 ordered that Khan be shifted to the privately run Shifa International Hospital after concerns were raised by his family and supporters over his health, including an eye condition diagnosed earlier this year.Instead, Khan was taken to the state-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) on the night of August 20-21 for a medical procedure and diagnostic examinations and was later returned to Adiala Jail.Uzma Khan's petition contends that this breached the Supreme Court's direction that Khan remain admitted at the Islamabad hospital until the next hearing on September 16. The government has defended the decision, citing security concerns.Two specialists from Shifa International Hospital also participated in Khan's eye examination at PIMS, according to the hospital administration, as reported by Dawn.Uzma Khan had sought an earlier hearing, arguing that further delay could affect the enforcement of the Supreme Court's order. The Supreme Court, however, rejected the request under its case-fixation policy, noting that 94 other criminal original petitions in the same category were pending, Dawn reported.The contempt petition is listed for September 16 before a three-member bench comprising Justices Shahid Waheed, Naeem Akhtar Afghan and Ishtiaq Ibrahim. The bench is also scheduled to hear other matters concerning Khan's health and family meetings.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
